edges.description: The exposed organism reaches mucosal surfaces where fibronectin binding can promote initial attachment to extracellular matrix and epithelial cells.
Adhesion is an upstream step that positions organisms for epithelial invasion and egress.
Barrier traversal moves C. fetus toward the bloodstream, where S-layer proteins support serum survival.
Serum-resistant S-layer-expressing organisms are selected for survival after bloodstream entry.
Bacterial persistence in blood is the mechanistic counterpart of the bacteremia phenotype.
Bloodstream infection enables metastatic seeding of endovascular and other secondary sites.

nodes.description: Ampicillin with gentamicin has been used successfully in neonatal sepsis from C. fetus infection.

evidence.reference_title: Abortion and perinatal sepsis associated with campylobacter infection.
evidence.snippet: As reported herein, one case of premature labor and neonatal sepsis due to Campylobacter fetus subspecies fetus was treated successfully with ampicillin and gentamicin.

nodes.description: Human infection begins after exposure to C. fetus from an animal reservoir, most plausibly by ingestion of contaminated food or water or by contact with reservoir animals and their environments.

evidence.reference_title: Campylobacter fetus translocation across Caco-2 cell monolayers.
evidence.snippet: Ingestion of contaminated food or water is a proposed route of transmission for both humans and animals.

nodes.description: Mycotic aortic aneurysm is a hallmark endovascular localization of C. fetus bacteremia.

evidence.reference_title: Campylobacter fetus bloodstream infection: risk factors and clinical features.
evidence.snippet: The main clinical features were fever with (62% of cases) or without (38%) extra-intestinal symptoms. These included mycotic aneurysm of the abdominal aorta (24%) and cellulitis (19%).

nodes.description: Bloodstream infection is a common invasive manifestation of confirmed C. fetus infection.

evidence.reference_title: Campylobacter fetus Invasive Infections and Risks for Death, France, 2000-2021.
evidence.snippet: Among 991 patients with isolated Campylobacter spp. strains, we identified 39 (4%) with culture-positive C. fetus infections, of which 33 had complete records and underwent further analysis; 21 had documented bacteremia and 12 did not.

nodes.description: Imipenem or meropenem can be used for severe invasive C. fetus infection.

evidence.reference_title: Campylobacter fetus bloodstream infection: risk factors and clinical features.
evidence.snippet: All patients initially treated with imipenem had a favourable outcome.

evidence.reference_title: Campylobacter fetus meningitis and bacteremia: A case report in a post-liver transplant and post-splenectomy patient and a restructured literature review.
evidence.snippet: Therapy was changed from cefmetazole to meropenem and vancomycin, then de-escalated to high-dose ampicillin.

nodes.description: Skin and soft-tissue localization can accompany C. fetus bloodstream infection.

evidence.reference_title: Campylobacter fetus bloodstream infection: risk factors and clinical features.
evidence.snippet: The main clinical features were fever with (62% of cases) or without (38%) extra-intestinal symptoms. These included mycotic aneurysm of the abdominal aorta (24%) and cellulitis (19%).

nodes.description: A rare but severe endovascular secondary localization of C. fetus bacteremia.

evidence.reference_title: [Campylobacter fetus subspecies fetus endoaortitis on a Bentall tube prosthesis. Apropos of a case].
evidence.snippet: Campylobacter fetus is a rare cause of endocarditis and endoaortitis: the authors believe this to be the second reported case of infection of an intracardiac prosthesis.

nodes.description: C. fetus binds fibronectin and can use soluble fibronectin to increase attachment to intestinal epithelial cells, establishing close contact with mucosal and submucosal surfaces.

evidence.reference_title: Fibronectin enhances Campylobacter fetus interaction with extracellular matrix components and INT 407 cells.
evidence.snippet: Together, this data suggests that C. fetus can bind to immobilized fibronectin and use soluble fibronectin to enhance attachment to other ECM components and intestinal epithelial cells.

nodes.description: C. fetus can cause bacterial meningitis in disseminated infection.

evidence.reference_title: Campylobacter fetus meningitis and bacteremia: A case report in a post-liver transplant and post-splenectomy patient and a restructured literature review.
evidence.snippet: We report meningitis and bacteremia caused by C. fetus subsp. fetus (Cff) in a 70-year-old man with liver transplantation and splenectomy for hepatitis C virus-related cirrhosis, on long-term immunosuppression.

nodes.description: Transplacental C. fetus spread can cause neonatal sepsis in perinatal infection.

evidence.reference_title: Abortion and perinatal sepsis associated with campylobacter infection.
evidence.snippet: As reported herein, one case of premature labor and neonatal sepsis due to Campylobacter fetus subspecies fetus was treated successfully with ampicillin and gentamicin.

nodes.description: Definitive therapy should account for high quinolone and third-generation cephalosporin MICs reported in Campylobacter bloodstream isolates.

evidence.reference_title: Bacteremia caused by antimicrobial resistant Campylobacter species at a medical center in Taiwan, 1998-2008.
evidence.snippet: The majority of the isolates were resistant to third-generation cephalosporins and quinolones, with minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC(90)) values of 32 mg/L for cefotaxime, 128 mg/L for ceftriaxone, and 32 mg/L for both ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin.

evidence.reference_title: Development of quinolone-resistant Campylobacter fetus bacteremia in human immunodeficiency virus-infected patients.
evidence.snippet: Relapsing C. fetus infections in quinolone-treated HIV-infected patients may be associated with the acquisition of resistance to these agents, and this resistance may be multifactorial.

nodes.description: Paracrystalline S-layer proteins on the C. fetus surface confer resistance to serum and complement killing and undergo antigenic variation.

evidence.reference_title: High-frequency S-layer protein variation in Campylobacter fetus revealed by sapA mutagenesis.
evidence.snippet: Campylobacter fetus utilizes paracrystalline surface (S-) layer proteins that confer complement resistance and that undergo antigenic variation to facilitate persistent mucosal colonization in ungulates.

evidence.reference_title: Campylobacter fetus surface layer proteins are transported by a type I secretion system.
evidence.snippet: The subunits of the S-layer are S-layer proteins (SLPs) that are secreted in the absence of an N-terminal signal sequence and attach to either type A or B C. fetus lipopolysaccharide in a serospecific manner.

nodes.description: C. fetus bacteremia can seed vascular foci, meninges, skin, bones or joints, and, during pregnancy, the placenta and fetus.

evidence.reference_title: Retrospective Multicentric Study on Campylobacter spp. Bacteremia in France: The Campylobacteremia Study.
evidence.snippet: C. jejuni and Campylobacter coli were associated with gastrointestinal signs, and C. fetus was associated with secondary localizations.

evidence.reference_title: Campylobacter infections in pregnancy. Case report and literature review.
evidence.snippet: Systemic maternal infection may present either as prolonged febrile illness or fulminant sepsis, and transplacental spread may result in abortion, stillbirth, or early neonatal meningitis.

nodes.description: C. fetus can localize to joints and cause culture-proven septic arthritis.

evidence.reference_title: Campylobacter fetus septic arthritis: report of a case.
evidence.snippet: We report a case of septic arthritis caused by the fastidious gram-negative rod Campylobacter fetus.

nodes.description: Serum-resistant organisms persist in blood, making C. fetus one of the leading species recovered in Campylobacter bacteremia cohorts.

evidence.reference_title: Retrospective Multicentric Study on Campylobacter spp. Bacteremia in France: The Campylobacteremia Study.
evidence.snippet: Among the 592 patients, Campylobacter jejuni and Campylobacter fetus were the most commonly identified species (in 42.9% and 42.6%, respectively).

nodes.description: C. fetus crosses model intestinal epithelial monolayers by entering and exiting epithelial cells rather than by paracellular barrier disruption.

evidence.reference_title: Campylobacter fetus translocation across Caco-2 cell monolayers.
evidence.snippet: Together, translocation without disrupting monolayer integrity, invasion and egression from Caco-2 cells, electron microscopy observations and the requirement of a functional tubulin cytoskeleton for translocation, support a transcellular mechanism of C. fetus translocation across Caco-2 cell monolayers.
